subtype: Approach: delays because the task feels too big [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Hrithik. This was last month, the day the history essay was assigned. Two thousand words, due in three weeks. I opened my laptop meaning to start, and my thumb found my phone instead. One video, then another. I told myself I'd open the file after this one.
The trouble was, I knew that the moment I opened it I'd see the blank page, and the blank page made me feel small, like the essay was a mountain and I was carrying a spoon. So I didn't open it. Three evenings went like that. The file sat on the desktop and I looked past it every time.

qa.q: How many words was the history essay?
qa.a: The history essay was two thousand words.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik feel small when thinking about the file?
qa.a: Hrithik feels small because the blank page makes the essay seem like a mountain and Hrithik a person carrying a spoon.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try to make the task feel smaller?
qa.a: Hrithik could split the essay into short parts and write a rough opening paragraph first, since a small piece is easier to begin than the whole essay.

qa.q: How might a teacher see the three evenings without progress?
qa.a: A teacher may notice only that no work has begun, without knowing that the size of the task was making Hrithik avoid opening the file.

grounding: A teenager scrolls on a phone and avoids opening a long essay because its size feels overwhelming.

subtype: Approach: delays because the task feels too big [Thinking]
passage:
School counsellor's note: Sachin, Class 11

Sachin came in on Monday because his history essay, 2,000 words, is due Friday and he hasn't started. He showed me his phone's screen time: six hours on Sunday. When I asked what happens when he thinks about the essay, he said, "It's so big I feel tiny. I don't even open the file, because then I'll see how empty it is." He said it without looking up. I asked him to name the smallest possible first step. He thought for a while and said, "Just open the file and write the title." Noor, his classmate, will sit with him in the library at lunch tomorrow while he does that. I will check with him on Wednesday.

qa.q: How does the essay make Sachin feel, in his own words?
qa.a: He feels tiny next to it, and afraid to open the file because he'd see how empty it is.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do after writing the title?
qa.a: Break the essay into small parts, like one paragraph per day, so each step feels manageable.

qa.q: How might Noor feel sitting with Sachin in the library?
qa.a: Noor might feel useful and a little responsible, glad to make starting easier for a friend.

grounding: A teenager with a long essay keeps scrolling because the size of the task makes him feel small, so he avoids even opening the file.

passage:
Thursday night

The project report is 15 pages. Fifteen! I opened my phone "for five minutes" at seven and now it's ten. My cousin Tenzin asked at dinner, "Started?" and I said, "Almost." Liar. Here's what I think is happening. Every time I imagine the report, I see all fifteen pages at once, and I feel like an ant looking at a mountain. So I don't even open the file. If I don't open it, I don't have to see how little I've done. Scrolling is easy. It doesn't make me feel small. Mummy called me "my clever boy, Akash" today and I felt worse. Okay. Tomorrow I'm going to open the file first thing, before the phone. That's all. Just open it.

qa.q: How many pages is the project report?
How does the report make Akash feel?
qa.a: Like an ant looking at a mountain; the size makes the task feel impossible and Akash feel small.

qa.q: What small step does Akash plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Opening the file first thing, before the phone, because starting is the hardest part.
Tenzin might not notice anything, or might sense that Akash is avoiding the work.

grounding: A teenager with a long report keeps scrolling because the task's size makes him feel small, so he avoids opening the file.
